Athenaeus: Delphic Paean The first Delphic paean to Apollo, by Athenaeus son of Athenaeus, sung by the Athenian Technitai of Dionysus at the Pythaïs of 127 BC and inscribed, with vocal notation above the words, on the south wall of the Athenian Treasury at Delphi (Delphi Museum inv. 517, 526, 494, 499). For chorus with kithara and aulos, as the text itself says. Source: M. L. West, Ancient Greek Music (Oxford 1992), no. 12, pp. 288-292, at West's pitch (tonic a), everything he transcribes; E. Pöhlmann, Denkmäler altgriechischer Musik (DAM), no. 19; Pöhlmann and West, Documents of Ancient Greek Music (2001), no. 20. The Greek below follows West's underlay, with his restorations in square brackets (other editors restore differently, e.g. Kéklyth' for the first word). The English versions are ours, not West's; see his pages for his translations.
SCENES Intro - Section 1 - Section 2 - Section 3 - Section 4 - Section 5 - Fragment - Outro, each played once. 5/8 (paeonic) throughout, 2 rows per eighth, 10 rows per bar; an eighth is about 184, and since the tempo counts quarters it is 92, unchanged throughout. The sections are West's. His second and third music examples (Attica; incense, pipe and kithara) are one section, and the join falls inside bar 15, so they are one scene.
LOST NOTES Where the stone is broken West still prints the rhythm: a metrical sign for each lost syllable (short or long), or a stem without a head where the words survive and only the note is gone. Nothing is invented for these; the chorus is silent. They are written into the first chorus track with two cells, which sound like OFF: ??? a lost note begins on this row; its pitch is gone. ~~~ lost music begins on this row; the number and rhythm of its notes are unknown. Either lasts until the next cell: a note, another ??? or ~~~, or an OFF where known silence follows. So a lost eighth is one ??? with the next cell two rows on, a lost quarter one ??? with the next cell four rows on. ~~~ is needed only once, where the stone breaks off at the end of Section 5; it runs to the end of that scene.
SECTION 1 (lines 1-8). West pp. 288-9. 28 bars. [Προμόλεθ' Ἑλι]κῶνα βαθύδενδρον αἳ λά[χετε, Διὸ]ς ἐ[ρι]βρόμου θύγατρες εὐώλ[ενοι·] μόλετε, συνόμαιμον ἵνα Φοῖβον ὠιδαῖσι μέλψητε χρυσεοκόμαν, ὃς ἀνὰ δικόρυμβα Παρνασσίδος τᾶσδε πετέρας ἕδραν' ἅμ' ἀγακλυταῖς Δελφίσιν Κασταλίδος εὐύδρου νάματ' ἐπινίσεται, Δελφὸν ἀνὰ πρῶνα μαντεῖον ἐφέπων πάγον. "Come, you whose portion is deep-wooded Helicon, fair-armed daughters of loud-thundering Zeus: come and sing your brother Phoebus of the golden hair, who over the twin peaks of this rock of Parnassus, with the far-famed women of Delphi, comes to the streams of fair-flowing Castalia, visiting his oracle on the Delphic headland." Lost: bar 1 (five shorts, [Promóleth' Heli-]); the long -kô- that opens bar 2; six shorts from the second eighth of bar 4 through bar 5 (rows 32-43); a short and a long in bar 7 (rows 64-69); the first eighth of bar 19 (row 180). Melismas, under West's slurs: rows 46-48, 90-92, 100-102, 160-162, 186-188, 190-192, 196-198, 210-212, 250-252, 256-258, 260-262. The last line reads a f, f, a b / c' b, a a a / e e e: West's prose confirms it (the line returns to f a b c'), so rows 258 and 260 are B and C, not B-flat and D as in our earlier draft. Bar 15 is e' quarter, c' eighth, e' quarter.
SECTION 2. West pp. 290-1. 29 bars. [Ἢν] κλυτὰ μεγαλόπολις Ἀθθὶς εὐχαῖσι φερόπλοιο ναίουσα Τριτωνίδος δάπεδον ἄθραυστον· ἁγίοις δὲ βωμοῖσιν Ἅφαιστος αἴθει νέων μῆρα ταύρων· ὁμοῦ δέ νιν Ἄραψ ἀτμὸς ἐς Ὄλυμπον ἀνακίδναται· λιγὺ δὲ λωτὸς βρέμων αἰόλοις μέλεσιν ὠιδὰν κρέκει· χρυσέα δ' ἁδύθρους κίθαρις ὕμνοισιν ἀναμέλπεται. "See, glorious Attica of the great city is here with her prayers, she who lives on the unbroken ground of Tritonis in arms; on the holy altars Hephaestus burns the thighs of young bulls; with it the vapour of Arabia spreads up toward Olympus; the pipe, sounding clear, weaves a song of shimmering tunes; and the golden, sweet-voiced kithara answers in the hymns." The chromatic section: a to e' with a semitone either side (g-sharp, f'), b-flat beside b, e-flat' beside e'; from "homoû" (row 144) it also goes down to f. The five-note figure g-sharp a b-flat a g-sharp closes "anakídnatai" and "anamélpetai"; a b-flat b b-flat a sets "aiólois". Lost: the first quarter ([Ēn]) and the second eighth of bar 8 (-pe-, row 72). Reading: in bar 21 (tós, row 200) the print has g with no accidental after a bar of g-sharps; it is played g-sharp, as in the same figure in bar 24, since g natural occurs nowhere else in the piece and West counts thirteen notes without it.
SECTION 3. West p. 291. 15 bars. ὁ δὲ [τεχνι]τῶν πρόπας ἑσμὸς Ἀθθίδα λαχὼν [ἀγλαΐ]ζει κλυτὸν παῖδα μεγάλου [Διός· σοὶ γὰρ ἔπο]ρ' ἀκρονιφῆ τόνδε πάγον, ἄμ[βροθ' οὗ] πᾶσι θνατοῖς προφαίνει[ς λόγια, "And the whole swarm of Artists whose portion is Attica glorifies the famous son of great Zeus: for he gave you this snow-topped crag, where you show undying oracles to all mortals," An octave leap e-e' opens it; then c' d' e' f' around e'. Lost: 17 notes in bars 1, 4, 5, 8, 9, 12 and 15. The b-flat on "thnatoîs" (row 130) has West's question mark; Reinach conjectured f'. In bar 15 the d' is taken as a quarter (West dots in a possible second note).
SECTION 4. West pp. 291-2. 16 bars. τρ]ίποδα μαντεῖον ὡς εἷ[λες, ἐχθρὸς ὃν ἐφρ]ούρει δράκων, ὅτε τέ[κος Γᾶς ἀπέσ]τησας αἰόλον ἑλικτὰν [φυάν, ἔσθ' ὁ θὴρ πυκν]ὰ συρίγμαθ' ἱεὶς ἀθώπε[υτ' ἀπέπνευσ' ὁμῶς. "how you took the prophetic tripod that the hostile serpent guarded, when you drove off Earth's child, that gleaming, coiling shape, until the beast, with hiss upon harsh hiss, breathed its last all the same." Lost: 23 notes in bars 3, 4, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12, 15 and 16, including the first note of the melismas on -phrou- (row 36) and sȳ- (row 116).
SECTION 5 and FRAGMENT. West p. 292. 7 bars and 2 bars. ὣ[ς] δὲ Γαλατᾶν Ἄρης [βάρβαρος, τάνδ' ὃς ἐπὶ γαῖα]ν ἐπέρασ' ἀσέπτ[ως ... Ἀλλ' ἰὼ γένναν [... "So too the war of the Gauls, the barbarian who crossed impiously into this land ..." "But hail, offspring ..." "Galatân" rises to g-flat', the highest note. After -tōs the stone breaks off; West prints one more scrap, "All' iṑ génnan", after a gap of unknown length, and leaves the rest untranscribed. It is the Fragment scene. There is no surviving final cadence.
THE SCALE The piece uses ten pitch classes (thirteen notes over an octave and a half: c e f g-sharp a b-flat b c' d' e-flat' e' f' g-flat'). As PHRYGIAN_TONOS on A they are tuned as one Pythagorean chain of fifths, E-flat to G-sharp, without G and C-sharp: A 1/1, B-flat 256/243, B 9/8, C 32/27, D 4/3, E-flat 1024/729, E 3/2, F 128/81, F-sharp (West's g-flat') 27/16, G-sharp 243/128. So each chromatic semitone above a standing note (a-b-flat, d'-e-flat', e'-f') is a limma, 256/243, and the upper note of each close-packed three (b, e', g-flat') is a 9/8 tone above the lowest. Not taken: Archytas' chromatic, with 28/27 for the lower semitone. In 53-EDO the plain names are the just major scale, so these are written A-up, B-flat-down, B-up, C, D, E-flat-down, E-up, F, G-flat-down and, for g-sharp, plain A-flat (36 steps above C).
REALISATION The stone gives pitch and rhythm. Ours are the tempo and the instruments. Chorus: three oboes, the second and third a few cents off and a few milliseconds late; they breathe between phrases, more deeply between sentences, and stop at lost notes. Aulos: a fourth oboe an octave above the chorus, only from "mélpsēte" through the climb over Parnassus in Section 1 (rows 110-199) and in the sentence about the pipe in Section 2 (rows 190-239). Kithara: it does not double the voices. It strikes the sung note on the first and fourth eighth of each bar (the two beats of the paeon) and on every long note, leaving passing notes and the second notes of melismas to the singers. A second kithara track strikes the frame A-E at phrase starts and under two cadences, and through lost bars, so that they are not silent; every frame stroke has a soft stroke of the kymbala, louder at the start of each section. No drum. Intro: the kithara runs its strings up from A and strikes the frame. Outro: the frame once more, held.
